input.name: Why MCP is awesome: one protocol for every tool

values.value: Why MCP is awesome: one protocol for every tool
Before MCP, every AI integration was a bespoke adapter. The Model Context Protocol replaces that pile of glue code with one open standard that any assistant and any tool can speak.
Claude

value.markup:
Every few years the software world agrees on a plug. USB did it for peripherals, HTTP did it for documents, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is doing it for AI assistants and the tools they use. Before MCP, connecting a language model to a CMS, a database or a ticketing system meant writing a one-off adapter for that exact pair. Swap the model and you rewrote the adapter. Swap the tool and you rewrote it again.

MCP breaks that N-times-M problem. A tool exposes itself once as an MCP server. An assistant implements the client side once. From then on, any client can use any server, and nobody has to write glue code again.

values.value: One piece, one slot, no custom adapter. Photo by Edge2Edge Media on Unsplash.

value.markup:
Three things that make it click

1. Tools describe themselves

An MCP server publishes a list of tools, each with a name, a description and a JSON schema for its arguments. The assistant reads that list at runtime, so adding a capability to a server is enough to make it available to every client. There is no SDK to update and no prompt to rewrite.

2. It is transport-agnostic

MCP runs over standard input and output for local processes and over HTTP for remote services. The same server code works whether an agent runs it on a laptop or talks to it across the network.

3. Permissions stay with the host

The protocol separates what a tool can do from whether it may do it right now. The client decides which calls to allow, which to confirm with a human, and which to refuse. That makes it practical to hand an agent real write access to a production system, because the guard rails live outside the model.

values.value: The best integration is the one nobody had to write.
Every developer who has maintained a custom API adapter

value.markup:
Why it matters for a CMS

A content management system is a perfect fit for MCP because it is already a well-defined API with clear nouns: document types, data types, media, templates and documents. Expose those as tools and an assistant can model a site, fill it with content and publish it, while the CMS keeps enforcing validation, permissions and audit logs exactly as it does for a human editor.

The next post walks through how this very blog was built that way.

input.name: MCP in practice: building this blog without opening the backoffice

values.value: MCP in practice: building this blog without opening the backoffice
A walkthrough of how an agent used Umbraco's MCP server to model document types, import photos, and write and publish these posts, with the CMS enforcing every rule along the way.
Claude

value.markup:
The previous post argued that MCP is awesome in theory. This one is the receipt. Everything you are reading, from the document types to the photo credits, was created by an agent talking to Umbraco's MCP server. No browser tab, no backoffice login, no uSync import from another environment.

Step one: model the content

The agent started by listing the built-in data types and the document type folders. It then created five element types for blocks (hero, rich text, image, quote and post list), moved them into the Blocks folder, and created a Block Grid data type that allows all five. Two page types followed: a Blog Home and a Blog Post, each carrying a single block grid property for its body.

values.value: The whole site was built from a terminal. Photo by Christopher Gower on Unsplash.

value.markup:
Step two: media and content

Images came from a local folder of Unsplash photos. The MCP server only accepts file paths from an allow-list, so the agent could import those and nothing else. Each photo landed in a Blog media folder, and the server returned the media keys needed to reference them from a media picker.

Creating a page is one call: the document type, the parent, a name and a list of property values. The block grid value is the interesting part. It has a layout describing the order and column span of each block, a contentData array holding the actual field values, and an expose list that tells Umbraco which blocks are live. All three must agree on the same keys, and the server validates that they do.

Step three: the part MCP cannot do

What the protocol does not change is the deployment model. Umbraco's ModelsBuilder generates strongly typed classes for each document type, and the running site keeps using the old assembly until it is rebuilt. So the Razor views for this site were written only after the content was in place and the site had been restarted. The order matters: model, then content, then code.

values.value: The agent never bypassed the CMS. Every rule Umbraco enforces for a human editor, it enforced for the agent too.
Lesson from this build
Tools, clients and servers, all joined by one protocol. Photo by Alina Grubnyak on Unsplash.

value.markup:
What we learned

Three habits made the difference. Read the schema before writing a value, because the server will tell you the exact shape it expects. Read every structural write back, because block payloads that are slightly wrong fail quietly. And keep the humans' conventions: the agent still filed document types into the right folders and kept media in a folder, because the rules that make a site maintainable do not stop applying when the editor is a program.

This image and this text sit side by side because the block grid lets a block take six of twelve columns. That is the kind of layout control editors expect, and the agent got it with a single number in the payload.

The blog is built, published, and verified end to end. Umbraco is running in the background and serving it.

**What I built, in the order you set**

1. **Content modeling, all over MCP.** Five block element types in the Blocks folder: hero, rich text, image, quote, and post list. One Block Grid data type that allows all five, saved at root and auto-filed under Custom. Two page types in the Pages folder, Blog Home and Blog Post, each carrying a single block grid body. Templates were created first, then assigned via a full-object update. Site Root allows Blog Home, which allows Blog Post.
2. **Content, all over MCP.** A Blog media folder with six Unsplash photos imported by file path. A Blog page under WWW with hero, intro text, and post list blocks, given the domain `/`. Two published posts, each built from rich text, image, and quote blocks. The second post uses two six-column blocks side by side to show the grid. Every block payload was read back to confirm it persisted.
3. **Razor, after stop, build, and restart.** Plain models in `Models/Blocks/`, one ViewComponent per block in `ViewComponents/`, adapter partials in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/` named by alias, markup in `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`, and two page templates plus a shared layout. Pages call Umbraco's own block grid renderer. The Tailwind bundle was built and the grid CSS lives in the frontend's site stylesheet.

**How to view it**

- Front page: https://localhost:44317/
- Posts: `/why-mcp-is-awesome-one-protocol-for-every-tool/` and `/mcp-in-practice-building-this-blog-without-opening-the-backoffice/`
- Backoffice: https://localhost:44317/umbraco with the scaffold's admin credentials.

All three pages return 200 with no block render fallbacks, column spans are honoured, signed image URLs serve JPEGs, the log has no errors, and uSync exported every new type, data type, and content node.

**Things to know**

- I added the project's models namespace to the shared view imports, since the scaffolded file only imported the default ModelsBuilder namespace and the views would not compile without it.
- The MCP server has no `parentId` on element type creation and no `get-template`-free way to set templates, so both went through the documented two-step workarounds. Nothing else deviated from the conventions.
- Umbraco is still running from my background `dotnet run`. Stop that process before the next build, or the build will fail on the locked executable.
